doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Free playing, time and the Classic Jazz Trio
title: Time in free improvisation and Charles Tolliver's band
summary: He explains how time exists in free playing, citing Tolliver's big band, and the college rule against jazz in practice rooms.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you’re playing in a free situation and you’re, especially if there’s no bass player, do you feel the — I don’t know if responsibility is the right word —
Taking time, playing time or something?
Time, yeah but you also could direct things harmonically if you wanted to it seems like.
Time is a fleeting thing. And it is a thing that it’s fleeting as well as it’s there whether you play it or not, you know what I mean? If I say [scats] [pauses] you still hear it, don’t you?

And I wait and do some other thing [scats] [pause] there it is. You see what I mean? It stays in the air. So you don’t have to keep playing it for it to be there. In between those things I can say hit a note and do a multiphonic [scats]. That’s time. In a free situation that’s time. It’s that time. It may be shorter or longer, each one of those phrases, but that’s time, you see what I mean?
Yeah. It’s a sort of a different way of codifying it, it might not have been four bars later that you decided to come in with that.

But that’s what I mean, you apply yourself to the situation and so therefore what the definition, how you define time, is different than how you define time in a twelve bar blues. This might be longer or shorter than a twelve bar blues, depending on where you start on it, but it’s still time. It is that time. I just heard Charles Tollver’s big band. And he does this thing, a phrase, it’s a phrase. But in that phrase he has elements. He has the saxophones going [scats] and he has the trumpets going [scats] and he has the trombones going [scats]. There is no ding-ding-ding — there is no time. But that is the time. And when that phrase happens that’s the phrase. Once they’ve played that and they start getting into the rhythm of playing those things, those elements, none of which necessarily relate tempo-wise to each other, but they still are the phrase. And from one time to another something may speed up or slow down but that is still the phrase and that’s a different concept of time. I mean after he’d played it once, I said oh, and I could feel the time, the rhythm of time of those phrases between each other rather than this phrase has some relation to the time and that phrase, it’s the relation of just them counterpointing each other that becomes the time you know. And so it varies according to the situation so that again, like I said, I don’t have a politic — a lot of cats have politic in music about the thirteen note, the twelve notes, and how/what order they go in you know what I mean? I got my first experience with that in college when they wouldn’t let us practice jazz in the © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

practice rooms you know? I said but these are the same notes I play when I do the Haydn Trumpet Concerto, why can’t I play like a bebop, so what’s the difference? “You can’t play that in the practice room, you have to get out of the practice room if you’re going to play that.”
